history: Água is Latin aqua with the qu softened to a g, the same change that turned Latin aequalis into igual. The word ends in -a and it is feminine: a água. In Portuguese it is simply a água, ‘the water’. Spanish has an odd rule here and says el agua with a masculine-looking article, but Portuguese has no such complication. In a café you will hear água com gás or sem gás, ‘sparkling’ or ‘still’, and água da torneira, ‘tap water’. Galician, Portuguese's closest neighbour, says auga. Latin aqua also reached English, but only through learned words: aquarium, aquatic, aqueduct. French eau is the same word, worn down over centuries to a single vowel sound.
historyEinfach: Água means ‘water’. It comes from Latin aqua. Over time, qu became g. The word is feminine: a água. In a café you can ask for água com gás (with bubbles) or sem gás (without). English words like aquarium come from the same Latin word.

elsewhere.text: The same Latin word, worn down to one sound: French eau is pronounced like the o in ‘go’.
English took aqua from books, not from speech, so it kept the Latin shape.
